summary: A 1970 note by M. Elie titled Getting rid of marking, about removing the marking field in the host-IMP interface. It is part of a discussion with RFC 67.

plainLanguage.summary: The note suggests removing an extra label on messages because it is not needed.

questions: getting rid of marking host imp
what is marking in network messages
how to remove marking from messages
subtitle: Removing unnecessary padding bits from network messages.

tldr.problem: Marking bits are added to messages for alignment at the sender's word boundary, but they create inefficiency in computation (messages must be shifted) and transmission (wasted bits reduce efficiency).
tldr.mechanism: Add bit counters to shift registers in the host-IMP hardware interface. The counter reaches 32 bits (one word), forces a word-complete signal, and resets, allowing messages to start cleanly at word boundaries without padding.
tldr.outcome: The proposed modification would eliminate marking bits while maintaining alignment, improving transmission efficiency from 7% to 10% for small messages and 28% to 40% for 32-bit messages.

today: RFC 64 is Unknown status. Modern network interfaces use more sophisticated alignment and padding schemes that are handled transparently by hardware, but the principle of minimizing unnecessary padding remains important for efficiency.

sections.title: The Problem of Marking
sections.content: Marking is a field in messages that indicates where the actual data begins. It was introduced so the message text could start on a word boundary in the sender's machine. However, machines have different word lengths (e.g., 18 bits versus 32 bits), so the receiver cannot use the marking scheme designed for the sender's hardware. Marking wastes bits in transmission and requires computation to remove.
sections.plainLanguage: If the sender says 'the real message starts at bit 4', a receiver with a different-sized word does not understand that numbering system.

sections.title: Inefficiency in Computation and Transmission
sections.content:
To process a received message with marking, the receiving host must detect the first 1 bit after the leader field, determine the shift amount, and shift the entire message accordingly. On a Sigma 7 (32-bit machine) receiving from an 18-bit machine, this takes about 12 microseconds per 36-bit word, or 1.5 milliseconds for a full message. This is roughly one-third of the time needed to translate the message into the host's internal format.

More serious is the transmission waste. A single ASCII character (8 bits) sent with marking, leader, and padding uses 112 bits on the network, for an efficiency of only 7%. A 32-bit control message achieves 28% efficiency. Removing marking would increase these to 10% and 40% respectively. Even for larger messages, the gain is significant—3% more efficiency for typical packet messages.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like sending a postcard with lots of empty space marked 'not part of the message'—the post office has to read and skip those marks, and they take up postage.

sections.title: Proposed Hardware Modification
sections.content:
The RFC suggests adding a bit counter to the shift register in the host-IMP interface hardware, starting at the beginning of a message.

From host to IMP: The counter increments with each bit sent. When it reaches 32 bits (one complete word), it forces a 'word complete' signal to the IMP, requests a new word from the sender's memory, and resets. This eliminates unused padding bits in the last word before the leader ends.

From IMP to host: A counter again counts to 32 bits. Once 32 bits have been received, the shift register is allowed to fill to its natural word boundary without accepting any new bits from the IMP. The next bit from the IMP becomes the first bit of the next word, which is the start of the actual message text.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of the sender marking where the message starts, the hardware automatically aligns the next message to start right after the last bit needed, with no wasted padding labeled as 'not part of it'.
